title: Silk production in China
summary: The earliest known woven silk dates to about 2700 BCE and comes from Qianshanyang in China. Early use of the domesticated silkworm has been traced back 8,500 to 5,000 years. Silk became China's most important export for much of its history and gave its name to the Silk Road, the trading network that connected East Asia to Europe, India and Africa.

uncertainty.note: World History Encyclopedia dates the earliest known woven silk fabrics from Qianshanyang to c. 2700 BCE; Science Advances (Fan et al. 2026) notes silkworm domestication evidence tracing back 8500 to 5000 years ago in ancient China.

as_recorded.value: earliest known examples of woven silk date to c. 2700 BCE & come from the site of Qianshanyang in China

where.modern_name: Qianshanyang site, Wuxing District, Huzhou, Zhejiang Province, China
where.historical_name: Qianshanyang, Lake Tai region, lower Yangtze River valley (Liangzhu culture settlement)

importance.justification: The Neolithic development of sericulture created a foundational textile technology and luxury commodity that shaped Chinese domestic economy and drove trans-Eurasian trade for millennia.

related.because: Neolithic Chinese sericulture produced the silk textiles that later became the primary prestige commodity of the trans-continental Silk Roads trade.
Silk produced in China was transported westward across the Chang'an-Tianshan Corridor network.

sources.title: Silkworm cultivation predating the Silk Road in southern Central Asia (2000 BCE)

reviewer_note: Dates for early silk use vary widely. Silkworm cultivation in southern Central Asia by 2000 BCE is why the record ends there. The pin marks Qianshanyang.
